name: Mbessa
world_status: statement found in an open source

earlier_scan.source_named: Only Glottolog MED for Mbessa [emz] is Paulin 1995, a 5pp wordlist; no grammar or phonology exists.

new_statements.quote: In addition, although Mbessa is a tonal language, in the Mbessa Language Committee (MBELAC), we do not mark tones on words except in a few special cases mainly for reasons of disambiguation. [...] Note that even for words where Mbessa and Kom have the same form, there are usually differences in pronunciation and intonation, especially at the level of tones. For instance, both languages have nawain for mother, but in Mbessa nawàin is pronounced with a falling tone on the second syllable and nawáin is pronounced with a rising tone in Kom.
new_statements.citation: Nsah, Kenneth Toah (Nsah Mala) et al. 2020. 'Rationale for Splitting Kom into Kom and Mbessa', attachment to ISO 639-3 Change Request 2020-028 (adopted 2021-01-15 creating [emz]). Dallas: SIL International (ISO 639-3 Registration Authority).
new_statements.locator: Rationale p. 1 (= PDF p. 6 of 18), opening paragraph and the paragraph before the tone-comparison table
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (18 pp., text layer present, extracted text). PDF p. 6 is headed "Rationale for Splitting Kom into Kom and Mbessa" and carries running page number 1; its opening paragraph reads verbatim "... In addition, although Mbessa is a tonal language, in the Mbessa Language Committee (MBELAC), we do not mark tones on words except in a few special cases mainly for reasons of disambiguation. Let us turn to the rationale for splitting the Kom code." and the paragraph after the four-language similarity table reads verbatim "Note that even for words where Mbessa and Kom have the same form, there are usually differences in pronunciation and intonation, especially at the level of tones. For instance,…
new_statements.rule_in_words: The language is stated to be tonal (lexical tone contrasts illustrated word by word: nawàin, Abàin, Akùin, Ibàin with falling tone on the second syllable vs Kom rising); nothing is said about stress or accent, and no phonological analysis is offered.
new_statements.exceptions: None; the author notes tones are left unmarked in the community orthography except for disambiguation.
new_statements.domain_note: Isolated citation-form words and short sentences; no word/phrase distinction drawn. Author is a native speaker and language-committee coordinator, not a phonologist; the document is an ISO code-change request, not a linguistic description.
new_statements.identity_note: The ISO documents and Glottolog agree on the identity: Mbessa/Mbesa [emz], glottocode mbes1239, Belo Subdivision, Boyo Division; until 2021 an Ethnologue dialect of Kom [bkm] (komc1235). Do not confuse with Mbesa [zms] (mbes1238), a Bantu C.51 language of DR Congo. The quoted source is by a native speaker of the Mbessa village variety itself.

sources.citation: Nsah, Kenneth Toah (Nsah Mala) et al. 2020. ISO 639-3 Change Request 2020-028: split Kom [bkm] into Kom and Mbessa, with attached 'Rationale for Splitting Kom into Kom and Mbessa' and a Swadesh-200 Mbessa/Kom list. Adopted 2021-01-15 as [emz]. 18 pp.
sources.note: Nothing on stress. Native-speaker author states 'Mbessa is a tonal language' and that MBELAC does not mark tones in the orthography; gives tone-marked minimal contrasts with Kom (nawàin falling vs Kom nawáin rising; Abàin/Abáyn etc.). No phonological analysis; no published linguistic sources cited for Mbessa.

sources.citation: Nsah, Kenneth Toah et al. 2020. ISO 639-3 Request for New Language Code Element: Mbessa (Iteanghe-a-Mbessa). 5 pp.
sources.note: Nothing on stress or tone. Lists all existing written material: Nsah Mala 2013 'Do You Know Mbesa?', Nsah Mala 2020 'Dictionary of Mbesa Names', unspecified BA/MA dissertations 'on different aspects of the Mbessa community'; states MBELAC is developing an alphabet (2019-).
Stub cites only Ethnologue; no phonology. Nsah Mala article confirms he writes in Iteanghe-a-Mbesa and lists no linguistic publications.
